newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-South Australia grain harvest under threat.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-South Australia grain harvest under threat.

text.p: An industrial dispute at grain terminals in South Australia could threaten receivals for the State's 1996/97 harvest, due to begin in early November, union and industry representatives said on Wednesday.

Steve Mahoney, of the Australian Workers Union, said industrial action was "a very real threat" following an impasse on an enterprise bargaining agreement between the union and terminals operator South Australian Co-operative Bulk Handling Ltd (SACBH).
"(Industrial action) is not our preferred course of action, but after nine months of negotiations, there has to come a time that someone bites the bullet," Mahoney told Reuters.
South Australian Farmers Federation grain section executive officer Michael Thomas said industrial action timed for the opening of the harvest could affect "hundreds of thousands of tonnes" of grain.
Thomas said a widespread dispute would affect receivals at Wallaroo, Thevenard, Port Pirie, Port Giles and Port Lincoln.
The Port Adelaide terminal, where workers belonged to a different union, would not be affected and could take some extra grain but would not be able to overcome the problem, he said.

"There is extra bunker storage on the Eyre Peninsula around some of terminals that could be used, so that probably would be fine, but there is not that luxury on the Yorke Peninsula, so (the dispute) needs to be resolved," he said.
South Australia is expected to produce 5.3 million tonnes of grain in 1996/97, according to figures released earlier on Wednesday by the State's Primary Industries department.
Thomas said the federation was supporting the SACBH in the terminals dispute, believing the cooperative had put forward an offer which was "more than reasonable".

There still was hope the dispute could be resolved before the harvest begain, "but I do believe it is unlikely (given) the length of time negotiations have been going and that it is an excellent bargaining time for the union," he said.
Thomas warned the dispute could become "ugly", saying farmers could try to drive their grain through union blockades.

Mahoney said union officials urgently were seeking further talks with the SACBH but if the co-operative refused to meet again or failed to offer a satisfactory outcome, industrial action could begin as early as next week.
